name: Umar Yilmaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start: tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm studying chemistry with a pharmaceutical focus, so it's lab days, problem sheets and a lot of coffee. I live in a flat share with two lads from my course, and I work nights stacking shelves at a supermarket, about 15 hours a week. My dad drives a taxi and my mum cleans offices, so they pay part of my rent and I cover the rest. I'm tired but fine. I came here to get a proper qualification, so I take it seriously.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called "AI Plateau". Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we'll see, but sounds sensible to me. I'd tell the lads that hype always runs ahead of reality. I'd say use the tools when they help and don't build your life around them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly I'd be a bit relieved. The thing I worry about is dad's taxi, because he's been telling me for years that apps took half his fares. If AI is hype, his job stays as it is, which is already hard. So it's not calm, just familiar.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on. I'd keep the night shifts, put about 25 a week away, and use AI tools sometimes for checking my chemistry notes, like I do now. I'd also try to get a summer placement at a pharmaceutical plant, because that's the most useful thing for a CV.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine. Not exciting. I like when things stay predictable, as long as the money works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which cost on your list worries you most while you study, and what would you do if money got tighter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The money's okay but tight. Dad's taxi income goes up and down with the season, and the supermarket nights are what keep me going. If Dad had a bad winter, I'd add two night shifts, and lab days would be rough on four hours' sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Think about the day you finish your degree. What do you picture yourself doing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I see myself in a quality-control lab at a drug company, in a white coat, checking batches of tablets. It's a good, steady job. With average grades I won't be in research, but QC is a decent living, and I'd be happy with that.

say: I'd say **hype** runs ahead of reality, so use tools only when they help.
I'd tell the lads not to build their lives around **technology**.
think: I'm relieved, but **Dad's taxi** is already hard, so it's familiar rather than calm.
With average grades I'd aim for **quality control**, not research.
do: Keep the **night shifts** at the supermarket.
Apply for a summer **placement** at a pharmaceutical plant.
feel: **Fine** and predictable, as long as the money works.
S0.quote: Dad's taxi income goes up and down with the season, and the supermarket nights are what keep me going.
fieldNote: Umar is calm because his course and plan feel **steady**.
His dad's taxi income is the **wobble** in the household.
He wants **quality control**, a realistic goal for his results.

steps.text: Keep the night shifts at the supermarket
Apply for a summer placement at a pharmaceutical plant

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called "Steady Disruption". Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's already starting and I'd see how it goes. I'd tell the lads to learn the tools that matter in their field. For us, that's lab software and data tools, not chatbots for fun.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think my future job is part thinking and part hands-on. Planning and reports would change, and lab testing less so. Quality control has a lot of paperwork, and that could shrink. I'd probably still have a job, but maybe fewer of them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take a stats and data module in second year, even though I don't love it. I'd learn the lab software the plants use. I'd keep the supermarket job, but I'd watch what the self-scan tills and stock systems are doing to hours. If hours drop, I'd look for tutoring chemistry to school kids.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not bad. A bit nervy, because it's the sort of change that's hard to see until it's already happened.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which jobs in your field, or the part-time work you do now, would AI touch first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The supermarket would feel it first. The stock system already tells us what to put where, and the manager says two of the nights could be handled by one person. That's my shifts. I'd lose about 6 hours a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would this change what you study, or how you study it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It would change what I pick. I'd make sure I have data skills along with chemistry, because the lab people who can do both chemistry and data are the ones who'll stay. I'd also ask lecturers how pharma labs are really changing, not what the brochure says.

say: I'd tell the lads to learn the **tools** that matter in our field, like lab software.
I'd say it's already **starting**, so watch how it goes.
think: Quality control has a lot of **paperwork** that could shrink.
I'd probably still have a job, but maybe **fewer** of them.
do: Take a **stats and data** module in second year.
Learn the **lab software** the plants use.
Look into **tutoring** chemistry if the supermarket cuts hours.
feel: **Nervy**, because this kind of change is hard to see until it has happened.

fieldNote: Umar splits his future job into **paperwork** and hands-on testing.
He plans a practical response: a **data module** and lab software.

steps.text: Take a stats and data module in second year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called "AGI by 2028". Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we're not ready and I'd say that plainly. I'd tell people to keep calm, but I'd also tell them to start looking at what they'd do. I'd say governments should spell out a plan, but I'd not count on them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be worried. If thinking work goes in two years, quality control paperwork and data checks go with it. I'd probably still have hands-on lab work till about 2031, but fewer posts. And Dad's taxi, well, self-driving cars are exactly the kind of thing that arrives with robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to my parents about what they'd do if the taxi stops. I'd keep the supermarket job and add more hours. I'd email a few pharma plants and ask what they hire for. And I'd think carefully about whether to carry on with chemistry or move to something more hands-on, like lab technician training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but I'd keep my head. I'm not someone who panics, though I'd feel it in my stomach.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your family, and what would you do about your degree place and your loan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut the extras, like the gym and takeaways, and save every spare note. I'd ask the careers office for honest advice, and I'd ask Dad whether he could retrain now instead of later. Dad's taxi is the biggest risk in the family, not my degree.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only two years, who or what would you lean on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd lean on my family, who'd lean on me too. I'd lean on my flatmates for cheaper rent. I'd lean on a lecturer I trust. And I'd keep a small emergency fund, because that's the only thing I can control.

say: I'd say we're **not ready**, and people should start working out what they'd do.
I'd not count on **governments** for a plan.
think: Quality control paperwork and data checks could go with **thinking work**.
Dad's **taxi** is exactly what robots and self-driving cars would take.
do: Ask my parents what they'd do if the **taxi** stops.
Email pharma plants about what they **hire** for.
Add supermarket **hours** and build a small emergency fund.
feel: **Worried**, but I'd keep my head and feel it in my stomach.
S2.quote: Dad's taxi is the biggest risk in the family, not my degree.
fieldNote: Umar's fear centres on his **father's taxi**, not his own job.
His response is **practical**: emails, hours, an emergency fund.
He considers hands-on **technician** training as a fallback.

steps.text: Ask my parents what they'd do if the taxi stops

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called "AGI by 2031". Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is good news compared with two, but I wouldn't relax. I'd tell the lads to use the time to get a real skill. And I'd say, steady as she goes, with eyes open.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be uneasy but manageable. I'd graduate in 2029 with two years before the AGI date, and hands-on robots about 2034. I'd have a few working years in a lab. Dad would be about 60, and the taxi could be pushed out before he retires.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree and use summers in plants. I'd save about 50 a week from the supermarket and pay the loan down early where I could. I'd learn the lab software and the AI tools for data checking. And I'd talk to Dad about a plan B for the taxi, maybe a job in logistics.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not great, not terrible. I can plan around it, which helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do differently in those five years compared with the two-year picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is a rush, five is a plan. I'd finish my degree, get a couple of placements, and have a savings cushion of maybe a thousand. That would make me feel like I had options if things shifted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: At what point would you decide to stay on your course or change it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd decide after the first placement summer. If plants are hiring juniors, I'd stay. If they're cutting QC teams, I'd shift to the data and automation side, because someone has to run the machines.

say: I'd say five years is **good news** compared with two, but I wouldn't relax.
I'd tell the lads to get a **real skill** with the time.
think: I'd have a few **working years** in a lab before hands-on robots.
Dad's **taxi** could be pushed out before he retires.
do: Save about **50 a week** and pay the loan down early.
Talk to Dad about a **plan B**, maybe logistics.
feel: **Manageable**, because I can plan around it.
S3.quote: Two years is a rush, five is a plan.
fieldNote: The **longer warning** turns Umar's worry into steps.
He sets a decision point after the first **placement summer**.
His plan includes **Dad's job**, not just his own.

steps.text: Save 50 a week and pay the loan down early
Help Dad plan a move into logistics work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth picture is called "AGI by 2036". Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, so don't panic and don't ignore it. I'd tell friends to keep learning, since that's the only advice that ever works. I'd say vote for people who plan for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be pretty fine. I'd be 29 and about seven years in a lab career. Dad would be 65 and retired. Robots for hands-on work come about 2039, and I'd have time to move into data or lab automation if I needed to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish, work in QC, and keep learning on the side. I'd buy a small flat with my savings and help Mum and Dad where I can. I'd use AI tools for work, because by then everyone will. And I'd keep a back-up skill, like programming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It sounds almost like a normal career with a long warning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does having ten years let you do that two years wouldn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With ten years I can do all of it, and I can look after my parents too. With two I'd just survive. Time lets me do the right thing, not just the quick thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a friend who's thinking of starting your degree next year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell a friend it's still a good degree, because science is real work and people need medicine. I'd say learn some data skills alongside it. And I'd say don't pick a course because of AI, pick it because you'd like the work.

say: I'd say ten years is long, so **don't panic** and don't ignore it.
I'd tell friends to keep **learning** and vote for people who plan.
think: I'd be 29 and seven years into a **lab career**, with Dad retired.
I'd have time to move into **data** or lab automation if needed.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because my dad's taxi and my own career would both be hit at once, with no time to react. What would help is honest advice from the careers office, a clear plan from the government and some form of retraining for people like my dad.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that people think students have it easy, but a lot of us are carrying our families a bit as well. I'd like someone to look at that.

headlineQuote: A lot of us are carrying our families a bit as well.
portrait: Umar is a **chemistry** first-year, 19, in a flat share, working nights at a supermarket.
His dad drives a **taxi** and his mum cleans offices, and the family money is tight but steady.
He is centrist and steady, uses AI tools now and then, and prefers **practical** steps.
He wants a **quality control** lab job and thinks about data skills as a back-up.
His real fear is his **father's taxi** being replaced, which sets his anxiety in the fast worlds.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** picture, because his dad's taxi and his own career would be hit together.
whatWouldHelp: Honest **careers advice**, a clear government plan and retraining for people like his dad.
